proof:
Under the formal substitution $\rho=1/\mathbb E e^{T/2}$, $p_0=1/b$, $t=1/2$ and $L=1/u$, one has $\rho=2/(2+u)$ and $h\rho=1/(2+u)$. Thus the two formal sides are the displayed $A$ and $B$.

Write $\epsilon=2^{-30}$. Then $\mathbb E e^{T/2}=(1-\epsilon)\sqrt2+2^{-10}$ and $b=2(1-\epsilon)+1024>1024$. The bounds $707/500<\sqrt2<71/50$, $\epsilon\sqrt2<1/1000$, and $2^{-10}<1/1000$ give $41/50<u<421/500$. Also $\mathbb ET=(1+39\epsilon)\log2>69/100$, since the first three terms of $2\sum_{k\ge0}3^{-(2k+1)}/(2k+1)$ sum to more than $69/100$.

Now $1/u<50/41<5/4$. By comparing fourth powers, $2^{-5/4}>2/5$. Consequently $\mathbb E e^{-T/u}>(1-\epsilon)2^{-5/4}>399/1000$. The numerator of $A$ is smaller than $1-(69/100)/(421/500)=76/421$, so $A<(76/421)/(399/1000)<1/2$. For the second bound, $(1+u)/(2+u)>91/141$ and $1-(1+u)/b>511/512$ since $1+u<2$ and $b>1024$. Hence $B>(91/141)(511/512)>3/5$. These final comparisons reduce to $152000<167979$ and $232505>216576$.

The two-point law has atoms and cannot be a sum of one or more independent exponentials with strictly positive scales, whose law is absolutely continuous.
statement:
Let $T$ take the values $\log 2$ and $40\log 2$ with probabilities $1-2^{-30}$ and $2^{-30}$, respectively. Put $u=2(\mathbb E e^{T/2}-1)$ and $b=\mathbb E e^T$. Then
$$
A=\frac{1-\mathbb ET/u}{\mathbb E e^{-T/u}}<\frac12,
\qquad
B=\frac{1+u}{2+u}\left[1-\frac{1+u}{b}\right]>\frac35.
$$
Thus $A\ge B$, the formal four-moment comparison at $h=1/2$, fails for arbitrary nonnegative laws with all four moments finite.
title: A two-point law refutes the arbitrary nonnegative Laplace comparison
